title: Taking pieces: is the capture safe?
outcomes: Finds a capture that wins an undefended piece
Checks whether the target is defended before taking
Knows that a capture is never forced and that a king cannot be captured

steps.text: You **capture** by moving onto an enemy piece and taking it off the board. A piece is **attacked** when the enemy could capture it next move. Captures are never forced, and a king is never captured: it is checkmated. Look at the target first. (The exact counting values come in the next lesson. For now: a queen has a higher counting value than a rook, bishop or knight, and each of those has a higher counting value than a pawn. "Points" means these counting values.)

steps.caption: The bishop takes a knight that nothing defends. Black cannot take back, so White has simply won a piece.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on e5.
Black has no piece that can take the bishop back.

steps.text: Before you take, ask: **is the piece defended?** A piece is defended when a friend could take back on that square. If it is not defended, it is a *loose* piece and the capture is free. If it is defended, you may lose the piece you capture with, so compare what you win with what you can lose back.

steps.title: Same capture, one change
steps.prompt: The queen on d4 could take the knight on b6. Predict first, then check. In the second position a pawn defends the knight; in the third a pawn stands nearby but defends nothing.

steps.text: **When it holds.** A capture is free when the target is loose. It can also pay when the target is worth more than the piece you may lose (*rule of thumb*; the next lesson counts the points). **When it fails.** A defended target taken with a more valuable piece loses material. You may always decline, and a nearby piece that cannot capture on the square does not defend it.

steps.prompt: Before answering each 'take it or not' question: what did you check first, and in what order?
